title: Contentment
hookLine: I have learned to be content
tomorrow: Pop's surgery runs long. what does love do in a waiting room?

cards: A gym shirt, a team banner, a phone wallpaper: I can do all things through Christ. It reads like a promise to win. It comes from a thank-you note written in bonds.
Paul is a prisoner, his letter to the Philippians says, and friends have sent him a gift.

He thanks them, then adds that he isn't saying it because he's in need: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.” So which is it: a line for winning, or a line for doing without?

teach.b: Read the lines around it first: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
Then: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.” Christians read that sentence two ways. The first hears all things widely.
Christ strengthens a person for whatever they're truly called to: a hard exam, a new city, a final with everything on the line.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: STRENGTH FOR ANY CALLING.
teach.b: Paul didn't fence the words in, and a believer facing something big is right to lean on that strength. The second reading stays inside the paragraph. All things means hunger and plenty, prison and freedom.
It's a sentence about endurance more than achievement: the strength to stay the same person whether the cupboard is full or empty.
Paul names that setting himself, and he says he learned it, the way someone learns a trade. Both readings agree on the hinge: the strength comes through Christ, not from the shirt.
And the letter to the Hebrews gives contentment its floor: “be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
Contentment rests on company, not on stuff.

how: Christians cultivate contentment through practices such as fasting, simple living and giving, and through prayer; some read Philippians 4:11–13 and Hebrews 13:5 together on the subject.

o: feeling satisfied once you own enough things
settling for less and giving up on hope
staying steady whether you have plenty or little

games.q: Paul's thank-you note — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says contentment came naturally to him
he says “I have learned” it, in plenty and in need.
'I can do all things' sits in a passage about hunger and plenty
it follows Paul's list: full and hungry, abound and suffer need.
Paul wrote this letter as a free man
he writes in bonds, as a prisoner (Philippians 1:13).

games.q: your teammate says Philippians 4:13 is about hunger and plenty, not winning games. state the other view at its strongest.
o: Paul didn't fence in 'all things'; Christ can strengthen a person for any real calling.
say the verse before a game and a win is guaranteed.
Paul wrote it about sports, since his readers loved athletics.
games.why: view one's best case: the words are wide, and the strength is Christ's. view two answers that Paul names the setting himself: full and hungry. both say the strength comes through Christ.

practice: Look at one thing you already own that still does its job: a mug, an old pair of shoes, a phone with a cracked corner. Keep your eyes on it and let it be enough for today.
If you pray, you can hold Paul's words: I have learned to be content.

wordCard.voice: Contentment. Being steady whether there's plenty or little: learned over time, and resting on God's company.

orig.note: the Greek word Paul uses for 'content' in Philippians 4:11.

carryVoice: Keep this one: content, learned slowly, in plenty and in need. Day seventeen thirty-nine, done.
